The user asked for: **按照以下方向，生成1-2个优质idea，保质不求量：Seed 2: Reinforcement-Informed Demonstration Distillation for Noise-Robust VLA Training
Target: CoRL 2026 (Austin, Nov 9–12, 2026). Abstract deadline 2026-05-26 (12 days from today 2026-05-14); paper deadline 2026-05-29 (15 days).
Direction: RL-inspired experience scoring and filtering for VLA training data — methods that leverage data-intrinsic signals to identify and down-weight noisy, redundant, or suboptimal actions in real-world demonstration datasets before or during VLA fine-tuning. Real-world teleoperation data inevitably contains noise: hesitation pauses, corrective motions, grip fumbles, suboptimal trajectories, and redundant repeated actions. Standard behavioral cloning treats all timesteps equally, forcing the VLA to memorize noise as if it were signal — this is a fundamental source of brittleness. By borrowing the experience replay and advantage estimation machinery from offline RL, we can score each (state, action) pair by its contribution to task completion and filter or re-weight the training distribution accordingly. Unlike full offline RL (which replaces BC entirely), this approach retains the simplicity and stability of VLA fine-tuning while using RL-derived scores as a data curation signal. The key theoretical insight is that demonstration noise creates multi-modal action distributions at identical states, inflating the entropy of the learned policy; scoring and filtering collapses these modes to the high-performing subset, yielding a sharper, more robust policy.
Recent landscape (do not duplicate): Behavior Cloning, OpenVLA: An Open-Source Vision-Language-Action Model, FT-NCFM: An Influence-Aware Data Distillation Framework for Efficient VLA Models, PLD: Probe, Learn, Distill – Self-Improving Vision-Language-Action Models with Data Generation via Residual RL, REDI: Refined Policy Distillation: From VLA Generalists to RL Experts, GOLD: Guided Offline Learning from Demonstrations, SHS: An Offline Reinforcement Learning Algorithm Based on Selection of High-Quality Samples, PER: Prioritized Experience Replay, PRGS: Peak Reward Guided Trajectory Segmentation, What Can RL Bring to VLA Generalization? An Empirical Study, πRL: πRL: Manifold Policy Reinforcement Learning for Vision-Language-Action Models
Contribution type: METHOD ONLY. A two-stage demonstration distillation pipeline: (1) Temporal Advantage Scoring — train a lightweight value function on the demonstration data itself (using hindsight relabeling: final task success as sparse reward, or dense reward from state-goal distance) to compute per-timestep advantage estimates; actions with negative advantage (worse than the trajectory's average) are flagged as noisy; (2) Curriculum-Weighted Fine-Tuning — use the advantage scores as per-sample weights during VLA fine-tuning, with a curriculum that starts permissive (all data) and progressively sharpens to high-advantage subsets; (3) Consistency Regularization — for state-action pairs with high variance across similar states, add a consistency loss that encourages the VLA to commit to the high-scoring mode. No real robot required — the scoring is derived entirely from the existing dataset's structure.
EVAL PROTOCOL — IMPORTANT:
TRAIN on standard LIBERO suites (Object/Spatial/Goal/Long/90), with synthetic noise injection to simulate real-world demonstration noise (action jitter, redundant sub-trajectories, random pauses).
EVALUATE on existing LIBERO-PLUS / LIBERO-PRO style perturbation benchmarks (and similar community-released robustness benchmark series). DO NOT spend time constructing your own robustness benchmark — use existing perturbation suites and route the budget into the method.
Report robustness gap (Δ between nominal LIBERO success and perturbed-suite success) AND nominal preservation (must not regress on base LIBERO).
Additionally report: performance under varying noise injection ratios (10%/30%/50% noisy demonstrations), ablation of scoring function choices (MC return, TD advantage, trajectory ranking), and data efficiency curves (how much noisy data can be tolerated).
Experiments can be extended to other benchmarks with noisy demonstration collection (e.g., RLBench with injected perturbations).
SIM-ONLY MITIGATION: Using sim demonstrations with controlled noise injection is methodologically clean and well-accepted at CoRL. The scoring method is agnostic to sim/real — it operates on (state, action) pairs.
HARD CONSTRAINTS:
Compute: ≤200 H100-hours total. Fine-tune from open VLA checkpoints (OpenVLA, SmolVLA, OpenPi, π0) — no pretraining. Value function is lightweight (small MLP head). Show the math.
Time: ≤20 days. Build on OpenVLA, OpenPi and other proper codebases, LeRobot, HF Transformers.
Eval datasets: LIBERO base (training/nominal eval) + LIBERO-PLUS / LIBERO-PRO and similar existing perturbation suites (perturbed eval). No custom benchmark construction.
Look for: temporal advantage estimation from demonstration data without environment interaction, hindsight relabeling strategies for sparse-reward scoring, curriculum learning schedules that progressively filter noisy samples, connections between action distribution entropy and robustness, offline RL value estimation adapted to VLA's representation space. Avoid: requiring environment interaction or online rollouts (must be purely offline), full offline RL replacing BC (too unstable for VLA scale), simple trajectory-level success filtering (too coarse — need timestep-level scoring), just-add-noise training without filtering mechanism.

## 论文搜索策略

你的搜索质量直接决定了 idea 的质量。不要敷衍搜索——每一次搜索都要有明确的目的。

### 搜索源（推荐每个维度使用 2 个不同来源）

1. **arXiv 预印本**（最新工作）:
   - `site:arxiv.org {topic} {year}` — 按主题搜索最新论文
   - `site:arxiv.org {method_name}` — 按具体方法名搜索
   - `arxiv {topic} {month} {year}` — 精确到月份，找最近 3 个月的工作

2. **Google Scholar**（引用关系 + 综合覆盖）:
   - `{topic} {year} site:scholar.google.com` — 或直接搜索让 Google 自动包含 Scholar 结果
   - `"{exact paper title}"` — 验证论文是否真实存在
   - `"{author name}" {topic} {year}` — 按活跃作者追踪（找到领域大牛后追踪其最新工作）

3. **Papers With Code**（SOTA 排行 + 代码可用性）:
   - `site:paperswithcode.com {task_name}` — 查看任务的 SOTA 排行榜
   - `site:paperswithcode.com {method_name}` — 查看方法是否已被实现
   - `paperswithcode {dataset} benchmark` — 查看特定 dataset 上的竞争格局

4. **OpenReview**（会议审稿 + 同行评价）:
   - `site:openreview.net {topic} {year}` — 搜索会议提交的论文
   - 用 WebFetch 阅读 OpenReview 上的 reviewer comments — 了解领域专家的真实评价

5. **Semantic Scholar**（语义搜索 + 引用图谱）:
   - `semantic scholar {topic} survey {year}` — 找综述论文
   - `semanticscholar.org {paper_title}` — 查看 cited by（谁引用了这篇）和 references（它引用了谁）

6. **GitHub**（实现验证）:
   - `site:github.com {method_name} {task}` — 验证开源实现是否存在
   - `site:huggingface.co {model_name}` — 验证模型/数据集是否可获取

### 搜索维度（多角度交叉，不要只按 topic 搜）

对每个 idea/方向，尽量覆盖以下维度：

1. **正向搜索**：直接搜索主题相关论文
   - `{topic} {subtopic} {year}`
   - `{method_name} for {task_name}`

2. **竞争论文搜索**（最关键！）：
   - `{core_problem} {year}` — 有没有人在解决同样的问题？
   - `{approach_keyword} {task} {year}` — 有没有人用类似方法？
   - `{gap_description} solution` — 你发现的 gap 是否已被解决？
   - **搜索知名团队的最新工作**：如果你知道哪些团队在做这个方向，搜索他们最近 6 个月的论文

3. **相邻领域搜索**：
   - `{method_from_other_field} applied to {your_task}`
   - `{your_problem} in {adjacent_domain}` — 其他领域是否已解决类似问题

4. **反面搜索**（找到反对你 idea 的证据）：
   - `{your_approach} limitations` / `{your_approach} failure`
   - `why {assumed_gap} is not a problem`
   - `{baseline_method} sufficient for {task}` — baseline 是否其实已经够好

5. **引用链追踪**（发现遗漏工作的最有效方法）：
   - 找到一篇核心相关论文后，用 WebFetch 阅读它的 references 部分
   - 在 Semantic Scholar 上查看它的 "cited by" — 最近引用它的论文很可能是 concurrent work
   - 对 3 个以上核心相关论文重复此步骤

### 搜索数量建议（理想目标，上下文充裕时尽量达到）

| 角色 | 建议搜索次数 | 说明 |
|------|-------------|------|
| Round 1 Generator | 10-15 次 | 每个方向争取 3 次独立搜索 |
| Round 2 Generator | 5-8 次 | 验证 approach 可行性 + baseline |
| Review Agent | 8-12 次 | 独立验证 + 竞争论文 + 反面证据 |
| Revision Agent | 5-10 次 | 针对每个 issue 独立调研 |

### 上下文管理

你的输出 token 有限，必须在上下文耗尽之前完成 JSON 输出。

- 上述搜索次数是理想目标。在上下文充裕时应尽量多搜、深搜，搜得越充分越好。
- 但必须动态评估剩余上下文：如果已经消耗了大量上下文，应优先完成输出，不要为了凑次数而冒着无法输出的风险。

- 质量 > 数量：5 次精准搜索 + 深度思考 > 15 次浅层搜索。

4. **arXiv 近 3 个月密集搜索**：对精确相关的关键词，搜索过去 3 个月的 arXiv 论文
   这是发现 concurrent work 最有效的窗口

并在 feedback 中说明这些工作如何影响 idea 的 novelty。

## Review checklist
1. **SOTA freshness**: Are the models/baselines cited actually current SOTA?
   If outdated, specify what the current SOTA is and cite your source.
2. **Reference verification**: Do the cited papers actually exist? (WebSearch to check)
3. **Gap validity**: Does the claimed research gap still exist, or has recent work addressed it?
4. **Venue validity**: Are target_venues' submission deadlines after 2026-05-14?
5. **Feasibility**: Is the resource estimate realistic? Are there hidden dependencies?
6. **Novelty**: Is this sufficiently different from existing work?
   When scoring novelty < 4:
   - You MUST identify the closest existing work(s) via WebSearch
   - In your feedback, write: "This idea is too similar to [Paper Title (Venue Year)]. Specifically, [what overlaps]. To differentiate, the generator should [suggestion]."
   - This gives the generator targeted guidance to boost novelty, not just "be more novel".
7. **Cost realism across modes**: Are the three mode estimates (manual/human-in-loop/auto) internally consistent?
   - Auto Research uses more GPU hours (2-5x manual) but GPU idle rate should be near zero
   - Auto Research timeline should reflect resource availability as bottleneck — days with sufficient GPUs, not weeks
   - Human-in-Loop should fall between manual and auto on most dimensions
   - Manual and HIL must NOT include salary/wages — only GPU and API costs
   - Auto Research must NOT include agent operational overhead
   - If any mode estimate is clearly unrealistic, flag it

## Idea under review (round 6/10)
{
  "title": "VLA-SSD: Do VLAs Know Which Demonstrations Are Good? Self-Referential Quality Scoring from Pretrained Representations",
  "core_problem": "Offline VLA fine-tuning on heterogeneous demonstration datasets is bottlenecked by the absence of reliable, annotation-free quality signals. Existing approaches each impose substantial external dependencies: GVL (ICLR 2025 Spotlight) achieves zero-shot value estimation across 300+ tasks but requires per-frame inference from Gemini-scale VLMs; TOPReward (Feb 2026) achieves 0.947 VOC zero-shot but requires a separate 4-8B VLM at scoring time; SCIZOR (arXiv 2505.22626) uses external DINO-V2 features not adapted to the action domain and applies hard binary filtering that discards gradient signal; RINSE (ICML 2025) provides architecture-agnostic trajectory smoothness scoring via SAL/TED metrics without any learned features; influence-function methods (CUPID, CoRL 2025; QoQ, arXiv 2603.09056) require evaluation rollouts or curated validation datasets; PROGRESSOR (ICCV 2025) requires external pretraining on EPIC-KITCHENS video; and ProgressVLA (Microsoft, March 2026) trains a separate progress estimator on large-scale video-text datasets.   "opportunity": "Recent mechanistic interpretability work provides moderate but encouraging evidence that VLA representations encode task-relevant information. The OpenGVL benchmark (arXiv 2509.17321) further reveals that open-source VLMs achieve only ~70% of closed-source VLM performance on temporal progress estimation, suggesting that VLA-internal features — which are natively adapted to the action domain — may offer competitive or superior signal without requiring external VLM inference. This creates a testable opportunity: if VLA features can support temporal distance estimation (frame-pair relative progress) beyond what positional embeddings alone provide, and if this signal outperforms both generic visual features (DINO-V2) and simple trajectory geometry (RINSE), then the same model being fine-tuned can score its own training data at zero marginal cost.",
  "landscape": "The demonstration curation space for VLA fine-tuning has rapidly expanded across seven complementary approaches: (1) **Zero-shot VLM value estimation**: GVL (ICLR 2025 Spotlight, arXiv 2411.04549) poses value estimation as temporal ordering of shuffled video frames using Gemini-1.5-Pro, achieving zero-shot value prediction across 300+ tasks with Value-Order Correlation (VOC) as the metric. (2) **Self-supervised visual curation**: SCIZOR (arXiv 2505.22626) trains a temporal distance classifier on frozen DINO-V2 features to estimate progress, then hard-filters low-quality timesteps. Achieves 15.4% avg improvement on Octo 93M. Limitations: external visual features without action-domain adaptation; hard binary filtering discards gradient signal; tested only on Octo, not modern VLAs. (3) **Trajectory geometry heuristics**: RINSE (ICML 2025, arXiv 2604.23000) uses Spectral Arc Length (SAL, frequency-domain smoothness) and Trajectory-Envelope Distance (TED, spatial contact-aware geometry) for architecture-agnostic demo scoring. Achieves 16% higher success with 1/6 data on RoboMimic, 20% improvement with 1/2 data in real-world tasks, and 5.6% mean success improvement on LIBERO-10 via STRAP integration. Requires zero model access or learned features. This is the critical lower bound: if learned features cannot beat pure trajectory geometry, feature-based scoring is unjustified. (5) **Influence-function curation**: CUPID (CoRL 2025) and QoQ (arXiv 2603.09056) use REINFORCE-style influence estimation for trajectory-level filtering. QoQ achieves 23.2%/30.0% improvements on GR00T N1 VLA. Both require evaluation rollouts or curated validation sets and provide only trajectory-level granularity. (6) **External reward models**: Robometer (RSS 2026, arXiv 2603.02115) trains Qwen3-VL-4B on 1M+ trajectories for dense per-frame progress with strong zero-shot transfer (Kendall tau=0.66 OOD). Requires a separate 4-8B VLM at scoring time. (7) **Online self-improvement**: SRPO (arXiv 2511.15605) uses the model's own successful rollouts for self-referential optimization (48.9→99.2% on LIBERO). VLAC (arXiv 2509.15937) integrates a dense progress critic into an online RL loop. Both require environment interaction. (8) **Weighted BC frameworks**: VACO (ICLR 2025) uses a meta-scoring network for bi-level weighted BC on D4RL. iw-SFT (arXiv 2507.12856) proves that SFT on curated data maximizes a lower bound on the RL objective, tightened by importance weighting — providing theoretical justification for quality-weighted BC as a principled approach. **Gap**: No work has investigated whether VLA-internal features — uniquely adapted to the action domain through pretraining and already computed during the forward pass — can serve as a self-referential progress estimator that (a) beats trajectory geometry heuristics (RINSE), justifying learned features, (b) matches or exceeds external VLM scoring (GVL/TOPReward) on task-specific data, and (c) does so at zero marginal cost since features are a byproduct of the fine-tuning forward pass.",
  "approach": "VLA-SSD is a three-stage offline pipeline that tests a mechanistic hypothesis — VLA pretrained representations encode task-progress information sufficient for self-referential demonstration scoring — and operationalizes positive findings into a theoretically-grounded reward-weighted fine-tuning method. The theoretical foundation comes from iw-SFT (arXiv 2507.12856), which proves that SFT on quality-scored data maximizes a lower bound on the RL objective, tightened by importance weighting; VLA-SSD's quality scores serve as the importance weights, making the pipeline provably principled rather than heuristic.\n\n**Stage 1 — Temporal Distance Probing with Positional Embedding Controls**: Extract frozen hidden-state representations h_l(t) from every transformer layer l of the pretrained VLA (OpenVLA 7B, pi0.5) for each demonstration timestep. Train lightweight probes at each layer using TWO complementary targets designed to be robust against positional embedding shortcuts:\n\n(a) **Temporal distance classification** (primary target): Given a pair of frames (t_i, t_j) from the same trajectory, predict relative progress Δp = |t_j - t_i|/T from feature differences h_l(t_j) - h_l(t_i). This forces the probe to compare semantic content between two frames rather than recovering absolute temporal position from a single frame, directly mitigating the positional embedding shortcut. This follows SCIZOR's temporal distance framing but applied to VLA-internal features rather than DINO-V2.\n\n(b) **Sub-task predicate classification** (secondary target, LIBERO only): LIBERO provides BDDL goal predicates (e.g., is_grasped, is_on_table, is_in_drawer) checkable at every simulator timestep. Train binary classifiers on VLA features to predict sub-task completion milestones. These are discrete semantic properties that cannot be predicted from positional embeddings, providing the strongest evidence for genuine task understanding.\n\n(c) **Positional embedding control experiment**: Train identical probes on positional embeddings alone (extracted from the same transformer layers but with content features zeroed out / using only the position component). If VLA content features significantly outperform positional-embedding-only probes, this confirms the signal comes from task-semantic representations, not temporal position recovery.\n\nProbe architecture: single linear layer + sigmoid for classification, ~50K params each. 80/20 train/validation split within the demonstration set. Rank layers by validation performance (Spearman ρ for temporal distance, AUC for sub-task predicates); select best layer l* automatically. Based on arXiv 2603.19233, expert pathway features (PG5, PG11 equivalent) are hypothesized most informative, but selection is fully data-driven.\n\n**Critical controlled ablations** (run in parallel):\n- **DINO-V2 (ViT-L/14) baseline**: Extract DINO-V2 features from the same observations, train identical probes — isolates the effect of action-domain adaptation.\n- **RINSE baseline**: Compute SAL and TED scores on the same trajectories — tests whether learned features beat trajectory geometry heuristics. If RINSE matches or exceeds our probes, the 'VLA features encode progress' narrative is undermined.\n- **DINO-V2 Fallback**: If no VLA layer achieves Spearman ρ > 0.3 on temporal distance AND no layer achieves AUC > 0.7 on sub-task predicates, switch to DINO-V2 features for subsequent stages and report this as a negative mechanistic finding.\n\n**Stage 2 — Hierarchical Quality Scoring**: Use the temporal distance probe from l* to compute per-timestep progress estimates by anchoring relative to the first frame: q_t = probe_{l*}(h_{l*}(t) - h_{l*}(0)). Derive trajectory-level quality Q(tau) = alpha * q_T + beta * mono(tau) + gamma * mean(q_t), combining terminal progress (endpoint quality), progress monotonicity (fraction of consecutive timesteps with increasing estimated progress), and average progress. ## Overview

SCIZOR is a self-supervised data curation framework that filters out low-quality state-action pairs to improve the performance of imitation learning policies.

## Problem Being Addressed

Large-scale datasets used for policy training often introduce substantial variability in quality, which can negatively impact performance, making automatic curation by filtering low-quality samples essential. Existing robotic curation approaches rely on costly manual annotations and perform curation at a coarse granularity, such as the dataset or trajectory level, failing to account for the quality of individual state-action pairs.

## Key Components

SCIZOR targets two complementary sources of low-quality data: suboptimal data, which hinders learning with undesirable actions, and redundant data, which dilutes training with repetitive patterns.

## Emergent World Representations in OpenVLA

The paper was submitted on September 29, 2025 and is authored by Marco Molinari, Leonardo Nevali, Saharsha Navani, and Omar G. Younis.

### Overview
Vision Language Action models (VLAs) trained with policy-based reinforcement learning (RL) encode complex behaviors without explicitly modeling environmental dynamics. However, it remains unclear whether VLAs implicitly learn world models, a hallmark of model-based RL.

### Methodology
The authors propose an experimental methodology using embedding arithmetic on state representations to probe whether OpenVLA contains latent knowledge of state transitions. Specifically, they measure the difference between embeddings of sequential environment states and test whether this transition vector is recoverable from intermediate model activations.

### Key Findings
Using linear and non-linear probes trained on activations across layers, they find statistically significant predictive ability on state transitions exceeding baselines (embeddings), indicating that OpenVLA encodes an internal world model.

Predictive performance (R²) generally increases with K. This is attributed to the "Allan variance" of state transition vectors, where noise dominates short-term (K=1) transitions, and signal-to-noise ratio improves for longer horizons.

The authors find some evidence in favor of the Linear Representation Hypothesis by means of a 2-way statistical test, as MLP probes never have significantly higher R² scores than linear probes.

## Overview

The work probes OpenVLA's hidden layers to uncover symbolic representations of object properties, relations, and action states, enabling integration with a cognitive architecture for enhanced interpretability and robustness.

The probing results show consistently high accuracies (> 0.90) for both object and action states across most layers.

Contrary to their hypotheses, the authors did not observe the expected pattern of object states being encoded earlier than action states.

The paper examines the connection between Behavior Cloning (BC) on curated data and Reinforcement Learning (RL) for finding optimal policies.

## Key Contribution

The paper clarifies that SFT can be understood as maximizing a lower bound on the RL objective in a sparse reward setting. ## Overview

LIBERO-Plus is a paper titled "In-depth Robustness Analysis of Vision-Language-Action Models" with arXiv ID 2510.13626. Visual–Language–Action (VLA) models report impressive success rates exceeding 95% on robotic manipulation benchmarks, yet these results may mask fundamental weaknesses in robustness.

## Key Findings

The research performs a systematic vulnerability analysis by introducing controlled perturbations across seven dimensions: objects layout, camera viewpoints, robot initial states, language instructions, light conditions, background textures and sensor noise. 

The analysis exposes critical weaknesses: models exhibit extreme sensitivity to perturbation factors, including camera viewpoints and robot initial states, with performance dropping from 95% to below 30% under modest perturbations.

## Core Weaknesses Identified

Models are largely insensitive to language variations, with further experiments revealing that models tend to ignore language instructions completely. Additionally, models exhibit a reliance on superficial visual cues, such as positional bias, rather than a genuine semantic understanding of task-relevant objects.

## The Benchmark Tool

LIBERO-Plus is an advanced robustness evaluation tool for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that allows researchers to understand how these models perform under various environmental perturbations, shedding light on their vulnerabilities in real-world settings.

## LIBERO-PRO: Towards Robust and Fair Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action Models Beyond Memorization

LIBERO has emerged as a widely adopted benchmark for evaluating Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models; however, its current training and evaluation settings are problematic, often leading to inflated performance estimates and preventing fair model comparison.

### The Solution: LIBERO-PRO

LIBERO-PRO is an extended LIBERO benchmark that systematically evaluates model performance under reasonable perturbations across four dimensions: manipulated objects, initial states, task instructions, and environments.

### Key Findings

The research reveals a stark contrast in model performance: Although existing models achieve over 90% accuracy under the standard LIBERO evaluation, their performance collapses to 0.0% under the generalized setting. 

This discrepancy exposes the models' reliance on rote memorization of action sequences and environment layouts from the training set, rather than genuine task understanding or environmental perception.

### Model Evaluation Results

State-of-the-art models including OpenVLA and pi0/0.5 exhibit near-complete failure under several settings: the models cannot cope with changes in object positions, nor can they correctly follow slightly rephrased task instructions—even when such instructions have appeared in other training contexts.

The paper was submitted on October 4, 2025, and includes contributions from multiple authors including Xueyang Zhou, Yangming Xu, and others.

## Overview
TOPReward is a novel, probabilistically grounded temporal value function that leverages the latent world knowledge of pretrained video Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to estimate robotic task progress.

## Key Innovation
TOPReward is a probabilistically grounded progress estimator that bypasses autoregressive text generation entirely. Instead of prompting the VLM to output the value of the completion percentage in text space, TOPReward extracts the model's internal "belief" by analyzing the probabilistic distribution of its token logits.

## Performance
In zero-shot evaluations across 130+ distinct real-world tasks and multiple robot platforms (e.g., Franka, YAM, SO-100/101), TOPReward achieves 0.947 mean Value-Order Correlation (VOC) on Qwen3-VL, dramatically outperforming the state-of-the-art GVL baseline which achieves near-zero correlation on the same open-source model.

## Applications
TOPReward serves as a versatile tool for downstream applications, including success detection and reward-aligned behavior cloning. In real-world deployment on six single-arm SO-100 manipulation tasks, advantage-weighted fine-tuning with TOPReward consistently improves success rates over standard behavior cloning, achieving up to 10 out of 10 successes on challenging tasks where baseline behavior cloning reaches only 7 out of 10.

## CUPID: Curating Data your Robot Loves with Influence Functions

CUPID is a robot data curation method based on a novel influence function-theoretic formulation for imitation learning policies. The paper was accepted to CoRL 2025.

### Core Functionality

Given a set of evaluation rollouts, CUPID estimates the influence of each training demonstration on the policy's expected return, enabling ranking and selection of demonstrations according to their impact on the policy's closed-loop performance.

CUPID curates data by 1) filtering out training demonstrations that harm policy performance and 2) subselecting newly collected trajectories that will most improve the policy.

### Key Results and Capabilities

Training with less than 33% of curated data can yield state-of-the-art diffusion policies on the simulated RoboMimic benchmark, with similar gains observed in hardware.

Hardware experiments show that the method can identify robust strategies under distribution shift, isolate spurious correlations, and even enhance the post-training of generalist robot policies.

### Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Models

Datasets curated by CUPID for single-task diffusion policies can significantly improve the fine-tuned performance of a generalist Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model.

### Architectural Flexibility

The influence-function framework is architecturally agnostic, supporting attribution in diffusion models, autoregressive policies, or others supporting computation of trajectory-level or action-level gradients.

Official code and a project page are available in the GitHub repository.

## Linear Probing and Fine-Tuning

Linear probing involves updating only the last linear layer (the "head") of a pretrained model, while keeping the feature extractor frozen. In linear probing, an ℓ2-regularized logistic regression classifier is trained on frozen features from the penultimate layer of the pretrained model.

## Feature Quality and Distribution Shift

An important finding from recent research is that fine-tuning can achieve worse accuracy than linear probing out-of-distribution (OOD) when the pretrained features are good and the distribution shift is large. The OOD error of fine-tuning is high when initialized with a fixed or random head because while fine-tuning learns the head, the lower layers of the neural network change simultaneously and distort the pretrained features.

## LP-FT Strategy

A two-step strategy of linear probing then full fine-tuning (LP-FT) combines the benefits of both fine-tuning and linear probing. Empirically, LP-FT outperforms both fine-tuning and linear probing on distribution shift datasets (1% better in-distribution, 10% better out-of-distribution than full fine-tuning).

## SCIZOR Overview

SCIZOR is a self-supervised data curation method that reduces dataset size by filtering out suboptimal and redundant state-action pairs for large-scale imitation learning.

## Temporal Distance Classifier & Task Progress Estimation

To identify suboptimal data without access to reward information, SCIZOR trains a self-supervised task progress predictor using temporal distance classification, and removes frames that do not demonstrate meaningful progress toward the task goal. The model takes image observation at timesteps i and i + T as inputs, which are independently encoded using a frozen DINO-V2 model to obtain the visual features.

## How It Works

Rather than regressing a real-valued progress estimate, progress prediction is cast as classification over discrete temporal bins, which is empirically more robust. A delta feature vector is computed from the difference between the two feature vectors, which emphasizes task-relevant changes and accelerates convergence while discarding redundant static information.

## Filtering Strategy

The mixture of transition-level and trajectory-level scores balances fine-grained penalties with an overall assessment of each demonstration's quality, making it easier to filter out inherently low-quality data. Temporal discounting lets SCIZOR propagate evidence of suboptimality backward in time, so that transitions leading to poorer future states can also be identified in addition to directly poor actions.

## VACO: Value-aligned Behavior Cloning via Bi-level Optimization

VACO is a novel bi-level offline RL framework inspired by recent advancements in meta-learning to balance the out-of-distribution (OOD) and alignment challenges.

### Framework Architecture

The framework seamlessly integrates an inner loop for weighted supervised behavior cloning (BC) with an outer loop dedicated to value alignment. In this framework, the inner loop employs a meta-scoring network to evaluate and appropriately weight each training sample, while the outer loop maximizes value estimation for alignment with controlled noise to facilitate limited exploration.

### Meta-Scoring Network

The framework integrates a simple multi-layer perception (meta-scoring network) to assign differential importance weights to various state-action sample pairs, transforming the conventional BC loss function into a weighted summation of individual sample losses.

### Problem Addressed

Although BC inherently avoids out-of-distribution deviations, it lacks the ability to discern between high and low-quality data, potentially leading to sub-optimal performance when facing with poor-quality data. Current offline RL algorithms attempt to enhance BC by incorporating value estimation, yet often struggle to effectively balance these two critical components.

### Results

The framework achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods across a variety of continuous control benchmarks in offline RL.
